
  One November afternoon, a letter arrived from the mainland. The new keeper would come in spring. Mara’s
  pension had been approved. She could leave whenever she chose.

  She read the letter twice, then folded it along its crease and set it beneath the sugar bowl.

  “I suppose that’s good news,” she told the empty kitchen.

  The storm arrived three nights later.

  It came from the east, driving rain against the lantern glass and lifting the sea until it slapped the cliffs
  high below. The wind found every crack in the lighthouse and sang through them. Mara made her rounds: lamp,
  clockwork, lens. She checked the fuel and tightened the shutters. At midnight, the light swept across the
  waves and found nothing but foam.

  Then the lamp went dark.

  Mara froze. The clockwork had stopped. She hurried to the mechanism, but the wind rattled the tower and the
  floor trembled beneath her boots. The spring had snapped.

  She fetched the hand-crank from the maintenance cupboard and set it into the winding shaft. For years she had
  kept it ready, though no one had needed it. She turned the crank. The gears caught, and the lamp began to
  rotate again, slowly at first.

  A flash appeared far out to sea.

  Mara leaned toward the glass. It came again: one bright spark, then darkness, then another. A ship was
  signaling. Its message was blurred by rain, but the meaning was plain enough. It had lost its way.

  The hand-crank fought her. Each turn jolted her shoulders. She kept at it, watching the beam cross the water.
  The ship’s light wavered in reply, sometimes vanishing for so long that she feared it had gone under.

  “Keep looking,” Mara whispered, though she couldn’t know whether the sailors could hear.
  The hours passed. Her palms blistered. The crank slipped once, bruising her thumb,
